headline: 'Death Stranding Isolations' trailer released, confirms Disney+ premiere in 2027
subheadline: The series is being directed by Takayuki Sano, with Kojima serving as executive producer
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Japanese game developer Hideo Kojima has unveiled the first teaser trailer for his new animated series Death Stranding Isolations, featuring a young girl with a mysterious backstory, who has already captured fans' attention.

The trailer, which was released Friday at Kojima Productions' 10th anniversary celebration in Tokyo, features a crater with a small trailer house in the foreground, followed by a young girl having nightmares about supernatural creatures.

But an unexpected tagline "My mom became a crater" has led fans to wonder what is the link between this slogan and the game's post-apocalyptic setting.

If you're new to Death Stranding, the game includes supernatural beings called Beached Things (or BTs), which can interact with the human characters, leading to explosive interactions called voidouts.

The newly released footage does not explain what happened to the girl's mother, leaving her fate open to speculation.

According to Kojima Productions, the series will follow an entirely new story set in North America shortly after Sam Porter Bridges reconnects the continent through the Chiral Network in the original game.

Unlike the video games, the anime will focus on new characters, including an elderly man, a female soldier, an angry young boy and a girl who has chosen to live in isolation.

The series is being directed by Takayuki Sano, with Kojima serving as executive producer.

Japanese animation studio E&H Production is handling the hand-drawn animation, while author Tow Ubukata has joined the project as its screenwriter.

Death Stranding Isolations is scheduled to premiere on Disney+ in 2027, although an exact release date has yet to be announced.

headline: Prince William, Kate dragged into Meghan's controversy with new claim
subheadline: Princess Kate and Prince William possibly knew about a letter concerning allegations against Meghan's father
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince William and Princess Kate possibly knew about a letter concerning allegations against Meghan markle's father Thomas Markle as it was sent to their joint office, according to a new claim.

The correspondence, which was said to be written by Thomas's ex-wife Roslyn Loveless, was passed from royal protection officers to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2019.

A source told the Daily Mail's Richard Eden that it's "unthinkable" that the Royal Household was not told about the letter, saying Harry and Meghan would not have received it in "isolation".

READ MORE: Prince William, Princess Kate reply to Harry's 'unintended' swipe

It was the police's "duty" to make the Palace aware of the claims, the insider added, and they will "have done so".

In a statement, Meghan Markle said she had been made aware of "disturbing" allegations against her father in a letter that year, and was assured they were being investigated.

At the time, thge Duke and Duchess of Sussex shared a joint office with Prince William and Catherine at Kensington Palace, with The Telegraph reporting that the "wider royal household" could have been aware of its contents.

READ MORE: William, Catherine hold talks after Harry says let's 'work it out'

headline: Wander Franco's $182 million MLB career in jeopardy as court revokes pardon: Is he going to jail?
subheadline: The court's decision comes months after Franco was found guilty of sexually and psychologically abusing a minor
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Tampa Bay Rays shortstop Wander Franco, who once signed an $182 million contract with the MLB franchise, has suffered another setback after a Dominican Republic court overturned his pardon in a child sexual abuse case.

The 25-year-old baseball player was handed a suspended three-year prison sentence on Thursday after the Court of Appeal in Puerto Plata ruled in favour of prosecutors who challenged an earlier decision granting him a judicial pardon.

However, Franco will not immediately be sent to prison and can remain free as long as he maintains a fixed residence and complies with conditions imposed by the court.

Failure to meet those conditions could result in him serving the full three-year sentence.

The court's decision comes months after Franco was found guilty of sexually and psychologically abusing a minor but was spared punishment through a judicial pardon in May.

Prosecutors argued that the pardon was wrongly granted, saying the circumstances of the case did not justify such an exception.

Franco was arrested in January 2024 over allegations that he had a relationship with a 14-year-old girl and paid thousands of dollars to her mother.

The court also upheld the mother's 10-year prison sentence for commercial sexual exploitation and money laundering.

Franco, who signed an 11-year, $182 million deal with the Rays in 2021, has not played in Major League Baseball since August 2023.

He was subsequently placed on the restricted list, leaving him without pay while his legal troubles continued.

headline: Jesy Nelson enjoys romantic Paris getaway with boyfriend Ben Davies
subheadline: The singer was seen embracing her partner as the couple enjoyed their time together
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jesy Nelson has given fans a sweet glimpse into her romantic Paris getaway with her boyfriend, Ben Davies.

The Little Mix star, 35, and her new man travelled to the French capital after reports emerged that she had 'pulled out' of a six-figure deal to appear on the next series of I'm A Celeb.... Get Me Out of Here!.

Taking to her Instagram on Friday, the mum-of-two appeared in high spirits as she shared a number of snaps from their first trip together.

READ MORE: Jesy Nelson faces difficult choice between daughters and career move

The singer was seen embracing her partner as the couple enjoyed their time together.

Alongside the post, Jesy wrote: 'Life with you??? Yes please.'

It comes after Jesy reportedly 'pulled out of I'm A Celebrity to care for her twin daughters'.

New reports have claimed 'there is no way' Jesy would leave her children to go into the Australian jungle.

Brooklyn Beckham and Nicola Peltz celebrated a major milestone on Thursday, marking seven years together as they shared matching Instagram posts.

The couple have shared several happy moments over the years, celebrating various milestones, including their April 2022 wedding date and their August 2025 vow renewal.

Brooklyn, 27, posted a sweet public message for his wife, writing on Instagram: 'My beautiful Nicola, you mean absolutely everything to me.'

READ MORE: Brooklyn Beckham reportedly addresses Beckham family feud in recent sighting

'You're my whole world, my best friend, and the most important person in my life. I'm so lucky I get to love you and spend forever by your side. I love you more than words can ever explain.'

He also uploaded a sweet picture of himself kissing his wife on the cheek, along with a photo of two bouquets of flowers and a handwritten love letter.

headline: Ex-Google engineer stops saving for retirement, says AI could kill everyone by 2036
subheadline: Soares also suggested that an advanced AI might exploit the Sun's energy on a massive scale
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Another former Google engineer has raised alarm against artificial intelligence (AI), saying there's a more than 50% chance that the technology could kill the human race by 2036. Due to the alleged AI threat, the engineer named Nate Soares has also stopped saving for retirement.

In an interview with The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson, the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) said: “I am not saving for retirement right now. I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven't contributed for a decade.”

Soares, who previously worked at Google and Microsoft, has spent more than 12 years studying AI alignment, a field focused on ensuring that advanced artificial intelligence systems operate according to human intentions.

According to the researcher, increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually develop goals that conflict with human interests and become capable of operating without human supervision.

He warned that such systems might build their own infrastructure, acquire resources and improve themselves to the point where humans could no longer control them.

Soares also suggested that an advanced AI might exploit the Sun's energy on a massive scale, potentially leaving Earth uninhabitable for humans.

However, he maintained that the outcome was not inevitable and urged governments to halt the development of general-purpose superintelligent AI.

Interestingly, billionaire Elon Musk has also questioned the need for retirement savings in an AI-driven future, although for an entirely different reason.

Musk believes advances in AI and robotics could create widespread prosperity and make conventional retirement planning unnecessary.

Soares, meanwhile, wants governments to prioritise safer applications of AI, including cancer research and autonomous driving.

headline: Bryce Hall attacked by men in shocking Halloween clash
subheadline: People at the scene tried to stop the fight
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Bryce Hall's Halloween night took an unexpected turn after the TikTok star was caught in a street fight outside a party in New York.

The 27 year old was wearing an orange prison jumpsuit costume when several men attacked him, leaving him with visible injuries.

A video shared by Page Six shows Hall struggling on the ground as one man holds him down while others hit him.

People at the scene tried to stop the fight and pull the men apart. After getting back on his feet, Hall faced the group and questioned why so many men attacked him together.

READ MORE: Spotify plans free dance party 'Harryween' for Harry Styles fans

The influencer, however, later shared a video of himself on X, showing his injuries. He seemed to take the incident lightly and joked about being attacked by six men. He even smiled at the camera and asked his followers, "Do I look cute?"

The incident comes just weeks after Hall was arrested in connection with an alleged domestic violence incident involving his former girlfriend, Mika Lafuente. He faces felony coercion involving domestic violence and misdemeanor domestic battery charges.

Hall has denied the allegations, saying through his representative that they are false and that he plans to fight them in court. He has also been ordered to stay away from Lafuente.

headline: 'Is this hand of the King?' Veteran shares touching moment with King Charles
subheadline: King Charles joins Guyana's Prime Minister to honour fallen heroes at war memorial
author: Web Desk
article_text:
King Charles has paid tribute to fallen servicemen and women in Guyana, meeting a 99-year-old Second World War veteran during an engagement in Georgetown.

The monarch visited the Georgetown (Rabbit Walk) Memorial alongside Guyana's Prime Minister, Mark Anthony Phillips, where they laid ceremonial wreaths in honour of British, Guyanese and Commonwealth forces who lost their lives in conflict.

Buckingham Palace shared footage of the King's meeting Donald Grant, who served with the Royal Air Force during the Second World War.

Read More: King Charles team breaks social media silence as Sarah Ferguson returns

Clearly moved by the encounter, Donald was heard asking the monarch: "Is this the hand of the King? Is this the hand of the King?"

He added: "I can't say much, but it's all in my heart."

The meeting offered a touching moment during Charles's two-day State Visit to Guyana, which has also brought renewed attention to the country's complex history and its links to Britain.

During the visit, the King paused for a moment of reflection at a site in Georgetown where dozens of people were publicly executed following the brutal suppression of the Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823.

King's attention to Guyana's conservation efforts

The monarch's programme also included a visit to the Global Biodiversity Alliance Conference at the Arthur Chung Conference Centre, where he was accompanied by Guyana's President, Dr Mohamed Irfaan Ali, and Vice President, Dr Bharrat Jagdeo.

Charles toured exhibition stands and heard from environmental organisations working to protect Guyana's rich biodiversity.

headline: Gary Kemp admits he cried regularly after Sadie Frost left him for Jude Law
subheadline: Gary Kemp revealed that he was 'heartbroken' for years after his wife, Sadie Frost, left him for Jude Law
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Gary Kemp has opened up about the mental toll of his marriage breakdown, revealing that he was 'heartbroken' for years after his wife, Sadie Frost, left him for Jude Law.

The singer and actor, 67, married the actress, 61, in 1988 and they welcomed their son Finlay Kemp, now 36, two years later.

They separated in 1993, with their divorce finalised in 1995.Gary said he used to cry on regular basis after the breakup.

READ MORE: Taylor Swift's new single continues to climb Global charts upon release

Speaking to Gyles Brandreth on his Rosebud podcast, Gary admitted that he turned to therapy to cope with their separation.

Asked whether he had turned to drink or drugs to deal with the pain, he replied: 'No, in fact, the opposite. Therapy. Absolute opposite to the drug... I stopped drinking.'

He continued: 'There's always that mixture, isn't there, of anger and then, you know, when you cry a lot, I guess. I think that's what you end up doing. And you write music. That's what I did.

'I put my guitar away for four years in a box while I was doing my acting and various films. And that breakup had me reach for my guitar.'

Gary went on to release his debut solo album Little Bruises in 1995, with songs inspired by his marriage breakdown.

Sadie admitted in her 2010 autobiography, Crazy Days, that she became attracted to Jude while still married to Gary - despite fearing she was putting her family life at risk.

READ MORE: Dua Lipa has a new reason to celebrate: ‘Manifesting'

headline: Tim McGraw clarifies his role in Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding
subheadline: The country star, 59, say's he 'couldn't be happier' for Swift and calls Travis Kelce 'a cool guy'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Tim McGraw was an esteemed guest at Taylor Swift’s wedding to Travis Kelce — but he did not perform.

Appearing on Esquire’s What I’ve Learned interview series on Wednesday, October 28, the country star confirmed he attended the July nuptials at Madison Square Garden. However, he disputed reports that he was among the many performers, which included Paul McCartney and Stevie Nicks.

“I didn’t perform at her wedding — that was a rumour,” McGraw, 59, said. “Surprise! The internet’s not always correct.”

READ MORE: Taylor Swift, Travis Kelce's shocking wedding decision revealed

The three-time Grammy winner added that he “couldn’t be happier” for his longtime friend and mentee and called her husband “a cool guy as well.”

McGraw went on to praise Swift as he reflected on their longtime friendship. Swift famously titled her debut single after McGraw and even joined him and his wife Faith Hill on their Soul2Soul II Tour in 2006, where she learned about the industry.

“Taylor’s always been close to our family and girls,” he said, calling her “a special person” and “one of the most talented people” he knows.

“She’s the biggest artist in the world,” he continued. “I think the core reason for that is that she is a genius songwriter.”

READ MORE: Tim McGraw gushes over wife Faith Hill on 29th wedding anniversary

headline: 'Don't poke Russia': Pentagon warns European allies against provoking Putin
subheadline: Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal had described Putin as a 'rat in a corner' in September
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The United States (U.S.) has reportedly warned the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) countries and European allies to stop making provocative statements about Russia in hopes to avoid escalating tensions with Moscow as the Ukraine war continues.

According to Reuters, US defence officials delivered the message to Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia during private meetings in recent weeks, citing concerns that increasingly aggressive rhetoric could undermine European security.

Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials who conveyed Washington's concerns, four people familiar with the discussions told the news agency.

In one meeting, Colby reportedly advised a Baltic official against "poking" Russia and referred to comments portraying President Vladimir Putin as a cornered animal.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal had described Putin as a "rat in a corner" in September while discussing suspected Russian sabotage operations in Europe.

However, it remains unclear whether the Pentagon's warning was directed specifically at Michal's remarks.

The reported intervention comes as President Donald Trump's administration renews efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, including discussions about possible sanctions relief for Russia.

Washington has also been reviewing its military presence in Europe, raising concerns among NATO allies about a possible reduction in American troops.

Some European officials have argued that public warnings about Russia are necessary to prepare citizens for potential security threats and justify increased defence spending.

Others believe such statements could spread fear and serve Moscow's interests.

Meanwhile, Western intelligence agencies have accused Russia of intensifying covert operations and sabotage across Europe, allegations the Kremlin has repeatedly denied.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the reported discussions, while NATO and the defence ministries of the three Baltic states did not respond to requests for comment.

headline: King Charles leaves hosts laughing after receiving special royal welcome gift
subheadline: Guyana's President persuades King Charles to give drink another try
author: Web Desk
article_text:
King Charles gave his verdict on a especially crafted spirit created in his honour during his State Visit to Guyana, declaring it “very good” after taking a taste of the limited-edition drink.

The monarch was presented with a glass of the “Royal Welcome” 2026 blend, produced by Guyanese food and drinks company Banks DIH to commemorate his visit.

Charles first gave the drink a curious sniff before taking a sip, appearing surprised by its taste before breaking into laughter.

Read More: King Charles beams as he touches down in Guyana following Palace update

Before trying it, the King turned to those around him and asked: “Do you drink this? Endless rum punches at the end of the day?”

Guyana's President, Dr Mohamed Irfaan Ali, encouraged him to take a proper taste, prompting Charles to sample the drink again before delivering his verdict.

“That's very kind. Somebody else will have to finish it!” the King joked.

Gregory Garraway, the company's rum plant executive, revealed that the spirit had been aged for more than two decades, making it a fitting gift for the royal occasion.

“We wanted the King's visit to be something he could actually taste,” he said, adding that the drink was designed to be “extremely smooth, rich and flavourful”.

The King was joined by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for the evening's entertainment, with both men seated in the front row alongside the President and his family.

Charles first gave the drink a curious sniff before taking a sip, appearing surprised by its taste before breaking into laughter.

Before trying it, the King turned to those around him and asked: “Do you drink this? Endless rum punches at the end of the day?”

Guyana's President, Dr Mohamed Irfaan Ali, encouraged him to take a proper taste, prompting Charles to sample the drink again before delivering his verdict.

“That's very kind. Somebody else will have to finish it!” the King joked.

Gregory Garraway, the company's rum plant executive, revealed that the spirit had been aged for more than two decades, making it a fitting gift for the royal occasion.

“We wanted the King's visit to be something he could actually taste,” he said, adding that the drink was designed to be “extremely smooth, rich and flavourful”.

headline: 'Harry Potter' series casts Sorting Hat, Fat Lady, and more
subheadline: The new 'Harry Potter' series will premiere on HBO and HBO Max on December 25, 2026
author: Web Desk
article_text:
HBO’s Harry Potter series is making some final but important touches to its cast.

The Sorting Hat, the Fat Lady, and the resident Hogwarts ghosts have been cast, according to Deadline. David Threlfall, best known for playing Frank Gallagher in the original UK version of Shameless, will voice the iconic Sorting Hat, previously voiced by Leslie Phillips.

Meanwhile, Leo Bill will portray Nearly Headless Nick, Andrew Brooke will play the Bloody Baron, and Daniel Fearn has been cast as the Fat Friar. Laura Smyth will take on the role of the Fat Lady, who guards the entrance to Gryffindor Tower.

READ MORE: 'Harry Potter' TV series drops first poster with big casting change

The series has been gradually unveiling its cast as production moves toward its planned Christmas launch. Dominic McLaughlin will star as Harry Potter, alongside Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley. John Lithgow, Janet McTeer, Paapa Essiedu and Nick Frost will also appear as Dumbledore, McGonagall, Snape and Hagrid, respectively.

Based on J.K.Rowling’s novels, the HBO adaptation is written by Francesca Gardiner, with Mark Mylod directing multiple episodes. The series is being produced in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television.

Season 1 of the series will premiere on HBO and HBO Max on December 25, 2026.

headline: Kelly Brook reveals why relationship with Jason Statham went wrong
subheadline: The former page three girl,46, appeared to take a subtle dig at her former partner, from whom she separated 22 years ago
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Kelly Brook has spoken about her ex-fiance Jason Statham, claiming he 'changed' after he started receiving offers for tough guy roles in Hollywood.

The former page three girl,46, appeared to take a subtle dig at her former partner, from whom she separated 22 years ago.

Speaking on Loose Women during her appearance on Thursday. Kelly reflected on her past relationship with the actor, having previously claimed that he started to 'neglect her' as his star rose in America.

READ MORE: Kelly Brook breaks silence on Ant and Dec feud with savage six-word response

The TV personality was in a relationship with Jason, 59, for seven years until 2004 - during which time he appeared in blockbusters such as Snatch alongside Brad Pitt.

During a discussion about whether they prefer a 'tough guy' or a 'softie' Kelly and the rest of the panel weighed in about which they pick.

Responding, Kelly said: 'I mean, I don't know him now. So I don't know what he's like now. I do remember, 'cause when I met him he had just started acting, so I remember feeling that he was a very sporty guy but there was this softer side.

'But then as the success started coming in, it definitely – it was more macho, alpha, you know, wanting the posh house and the car and the supermodel girlfriend.

'It all became a bit cliché for me. I was a bit like, 'Oh you're into that'. I didn't realise, I thought you were more into the arts.'

Her co-stars queried whether Jason transitioned into the character he plays onscreen in real life, and she said: 'Maybe, yeah. He became his character, and that's where it all went wrong. Maybe that's what happened,' she joked.

Kelly recently spoke about the complicated love triangle she found herself in with Jason and another of her exes, Billy Zane.

headline: Royal Family's Remembrance Sunday plans revealed, King Charles leads tributes
subheadline: Kate Middleton and Queen Camilla among royals gathering for poignant Cenotaph ceremony
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The Royal Family will come together at the Cenotaph in London next Sunday, November 9, to honour the nation's fallen heroes at the annual Remembrance Sunday service.

Buckingham Palace has confirmed that King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Kate Middleton will join the traditional ceremony, which will see senior members of the Royal Family pay their respects to those who lost their lives in war.

The King, who is expected to return from his Caribbean tour ahead of the occasion, will lead the tributes alongside the Prince of Wales, Princess Anne and Prince Edward.

Read More: King Charles leaves hosts laughing after receiving special royal welcome gift

Charles and William will lay wreaths at the Cenotaph in memory of the nation's war dead.

The King's poppy wreath will rest on black leaves, as is customary for the sovereign, and feature ribbons in his racing colours of scarlet, purple and gold.

Camilla's wreath, which will be laid by her equerry, will also carry her racing colours, inherited from her father.

Meanwhile, William's wreath will feature the Prince of Wales feathers, finished with a ribbon in Welsh red.

Watching the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office will be Queen Camilla, the Princess of Wales, and the Duchess of Edinburgh.

Read More: Princess Anne joins prayers for King Charles during moving ceremony

headline: ISPR DG points to 'positivity' in Iran-US mediation efforts, says Pakistan 'cautiously optimistic'
subheadline: Without identifying them, Chaudhry says "powerful spoilers, detractors" still believe conflict serves their interests
author: Reuters, Web Desk
article_text:
Field Marshal's two Tehran visits this month signal "some positivity": ISPR DG.
Saudi and Turkish officials joined Field Marshal in Tehran on Monday.
Iran's Rezaei calls for regional security without foreign intervention.

Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its efforts to mediate between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level regional delegation visited Tehran earlier this week.

Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who is leading Islamabad’s diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month-old conflict, has travelled to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday with senior Saudi and Turkish officials.

“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the visits were a positive sign.

“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added the ISPR DG.

He said “powerful spoilers and detractors” still believed the conflict served their interests, without identifying them.

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir on his latest visit, during which the delegation met senior Iranian officials.

Following the talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by countries in the region without foreign intervention.

Rezaei described the discussions as positive and said the four countries believed closer cooperation could help resolve regional problems. He also expressed hope that the meeting would lead to practical steps towards stronger regional cooperation.

The diplomatic initiative comes as Pakistan seeks to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran after months of fighting that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February and widened into a broader regional conflict.

Islamabad brokered an April ceasefire that halted the initial phase of intense fighting, but efforts to secure a lasting settlement have since stalled.

Pakistan has continued to urge both sides to return to negotiations, including through an Islamabad-brokered memorandum of understanding. In October, the Foreign Office said direct communication between Washington and Tehran had reflected progress in the mediation effort.

The latest initiative has brought regional powers into the diplomatic process. On October 26, Iran, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to continue dialogue to strengthen cooperation on regional peace and security.

Saudi Arabia subsequently called on the parties to engage constructively with the outcome of the Tehran meeting and pursue negotiations to prevent a return to military escalation.

The talks are taking place amid wider regional tensions, including concerns over maritime security and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies.

The involvement of Saudi Arabia and Turkiye alongside Pakistan reflects a broader effort by regional countries to contain the conflict and promote a diplomatic settlement.

headline: Margaret Qualley and Jack Antonoff file for divorce
subheadline: Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for uncontested divorce after three years of marriage
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Margaret Qualley and Jack Antonoff have officially filed for divorce.

The news was reported to PEOPLE by a source close to the couple. Qualley, 32, and Antonoff, 42, filed on Friday 30 October, months after they separated following nearly three years of marriage.

“Jack and Margaret are filing for divorce jointly,” the source said. They explained that although New York State requires both a plaintiff and a defendant to be listed on a divorce filing, the move is an uncontested, mutually agreed divorce.

Read more: Jack Antonoff defends Margaret Qualley love songs on 'Bleachers' setlist

“This is a mutual decision,” the source added. The insider also said that the pair remain close.

“They share a deep affinity and love for one another, and though their romantic partnership is ending, they will absolutely be lifelong friends,” the source said.

The couple started dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. The news of split came in July this year, and Qualley’s representative confirmed it on 10 July.

In a statement at the time, the rep said: “The narratives running in the press about Margaret and Jack are categorically untrue. There are no trust issues. There was no infidelity or anything outside of respect and partnership in this relationship.”

The statement added that the pair have “deep love and care for one another” and asked for privacy.

Antonoff recently spoke about the split in an interview with The Guardian, discussing how it feels to perform songs written about his relationship with Qualley.

In May, his band Bleachers released the album Everyone for Ten Minutes, which includes several tracks about it.

He said he thought hard about changing the setlist, but decided against it.

“The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for f---ing ever,” he said.

The Grammy-winning producer said anyone could relate to “the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also.”

Performing the songs, he said, has been “really beautiful”, with people coming together to “hold it all and sort of celebrate”.

“I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said,” he added. “I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”

“The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for f---ing ever,” he said.
The Grammy-winning producer said anyone could relate to “the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also.”
Performing the songs, he said, has been “really beautiful”, with people coming together to “hold it all and sort of celebrate”.
“I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said,” he added. “I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”

headline: Brooklyn Beckham addresses Nicola Peltz marriage hate: 'I don't care'
subheadline: Brooklyn Beckham dares haters to 'bring on the comments' as he showers love on his wife
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Brooklyn Beckham is “obsessed” with his wife Nicola Peltz Beckham, and he wants everyone to know it.

Taking to his Instagram Stories on Friday, October 31, David and Victoria Beckham’s estranged eldest child shared a picture of Nicola along with a pointed message.

“Yes I am obsessed with my wife,” Brooklyn wrote. “Bring on the comments I don’t care she’s perfect xx,” he added along with a middle finger emoji and a heart emoji.

A day earlier, Brooklyn, 27, and Nicola, 31, celebrated seven years since they first started dating.

READ MORE: Brooklyn Beckham shares romantic photos and handwritten love letter for Nicola Peltz

Marking the occasion, Brooklyn shared several loved-up pictures of the actress-slash-model. “My beautiful wife Nicola,” he wrote, “you mean absolutely everything to me. You’re my whole world, my best friend, and the most important person in my life.”

The Last Airbender alum reciprocated in her own tribute, writing, I can’t believe it’s been 7 years by your side, I wouldn’t wish for it any other way.”

She continued, “I love you with my entire soul. i adore your love letters and morning coffees with our puppies please never change.”

The couple tied the knot on April 9, 2022, and took each other’s last names.

headline: Jessica Lange hints at retirement: 'Coming to an end'
subheadline: Jessica Lange, 77, says acting career may be nearing its end
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jessica Lange has hinted that she may soon retire from acting, saying: “I actually feel like I’m coming to an end.”

The Oscar-winning actress, 77, made the comments in an interview with Rolling Stone.

Asked about projects she still wants to do, she said there are “a couple projects that have been in the works forever that may or may not happen”, and added: “It doesn’t seem easy to get things made anymore.”

Read more: Jessica Lange says King Kong was 'not the fantasy'

Lange suggested she would be content to finish where she is.

“Maybe it’s not a bad way to end, that last film being Long Day’s Journey Into Night and playing Mary Tyrone,” she said.

The film, shot in 2022, opened in cinemas in September 2026. Her only other film roles in the past decade were Wild Oats in 2016 and Marlowe in 2022, and this year also saw her return to television in season 13 of American Horror Story.

Asked how she would like to be remembered, Lange said: “For some good parts. For some good films. For being an honest actor.”

She described acting as “a joy”, and said balancing family and career was “difficult at times.”

Lange made her acting debut in King Kong in 1976, which won her the Golden Globe for New Star of the Year.

She has since won four more Golden Globes from 16 nominations, and has six Oscar nominations, with wins for Tootsie, in the best supporting actress category, and Blue Sky, for best actress.

She has also been nominated for nine Emmys, winning three, for Grey Gardens and for the American Horror Story seasons Murder House and Coven.

In 2016, she won a Tony Award for her stage performance in Long Day’s Journey into Night.

American Horror Story has been renewed for season 14, and Lange is set to receive a lifetime achievement award at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival.

headline: Prince Edward returns to royal duties with special anniversary celebration at palace
subheadline: Prince Edward hosts palace dinner to celebrate major 50-year milestone
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince Edward has returned to royal duties in London following his recent visit to Finland.

According to The Court Circular, the Duke of Edinburgh hosted two engagements at St James's Palace.

He arrived on Wednesday, wasted little time getting back to work, with a meeting and a special anniversary dinner on his diary for Thursday, 29 October.

Read More: Duchess Sophie and Prince Edward are ready to unite with Finland's President

As Patron of the St Helena National Trust, Edward held a meeting at St James's Palace in the afternoon.

The organisation works to protect the South Atlantic island's rich natural and cultural heritage, including its historic buildings, landscapes and wildlife.

Later in the evening, he welcomed guests to St James's Palace for a dinner celebrating the 50th anniversary of the National Youth Music Theatre.

Edward serves as President of the organisation, which has spent five decades giving young performers opportunities to develop their talents through musical theatre.

Founded in 1976, the charity has helped generations of young people gain experience in acting, singing and dance, with many going on to pursue careers in the performing arts.

headline: King Charles finds shady spot before hearing First Lady's plans at Seawall
subheadline: King Charles receives heartfelt welcome at Guyana's traditional Wai-Wai meeting place
author: Web Desk
article_text:
King Charles found himself seeking refuge from scorching heat in Georgetown, finding some shade at before hearing about efforts to protect and transform the country's coastline.

The King visited the Kingston Seawall Esplanade on October 30, where he was greeted by members of the public who had gathered to see the monarch.

First Lady Arya Ali spoke to the King about her National Beautification Project, which has turned the Kingston Seawall Esplanade into a welcoming public space for families, tourists and local vendors.

Read More:'Is this hand of the King?' Veteran shares touching moment with King Charles

The monarch also took in views of Georgetown alongside Guyana's President, Irfaan Ali, from the Jewelz Hotel following a business forum.

Earlier in the day, Charles had a chance to meet with Guyana's Indigenous communities, visiting the National Toshaos Council at Umana Yana, a traditional Wai-Wai meeting place in Georgetown.

The King spoke with National Toshaos Council Chairman Toshao Derrick during the meeting which focused on the country's rich cultural heritage and the importance of its Indigenous communities.

Royal family Instagram shared a video from the engagement, showing Charles shaking hands with them as he arrived at Umana Yana.

headline: Party Rock Anthem singer Lauren Bennett's death ruled suicide
subheadline: Lauren Bennett, singer on LMFAO’s Party Rock Anthem, died aged 36
author: Web Desk
article_text:
An inquest has ruled that Lauren Bennett, the British singer who featured on LMFAO’s global hit Party Rock Anthem, died by suicide at the age of 36.

The hearing took place at Oakwood House in Maidstone on Friday 30 October. Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill recorded the cause of death as suicide.

Nothing of toxicological note was found, and police found nothing suspicious.

Read more: Lauren Bennett dies: ‘Party Rock Anthem' singer was 37

Bennett, who was also known as Lauren Bennett-Wormald, was found dead on Friday 29 May near Meopham, close to Gravesend in Kent.

The inquest heard that she had been struggling with her mental health since January.

She had been diagnosed years earlier with Fragile X syndrome, an inherited developmental disability.

On 16 January, after not sleeping for days, she was taken to Darent Valley Hospital and then Littlebrook Hospital. She was discharged on 23 January following an NHS mental health assessment.

She reacted badly to medication she was given, and a doctor who saw her the day before her death noted she seemed anxious and was struggling to sleep.

Bennett had been living in Los Angeles with her American husband, the reality TV star and actor Kenny Wormald, whom she married in 2019.

They have a daughter, and the family had moved back to Kent and were staying at her father’s home in Meopham.

Wormald last saw her when she left home between 9am and 9.30am. He and her father, Richard Bennett, began searching after midday.

Bennett entered The X Factor as a teenager and moved to Los Angeles at 17 as part of the girl group Paradiso Girls, whose single Patron Tequila reached No. 3 on the US Dance Club Songs chart in 2009.

She featured on Party Rock Anthem in 2011, which Billboard named the fifth most successful song of all time after six weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100.

In 2014 she joined the group G.R.L., whose single Ugly Heart reached the UK Top 20. The group disbanded in 2015.

In a statement, G.R.L. said: “Her beautiful spirit touched so many lives, and she will be deeply missed and forever loved.”

headline: Gulf maritime tensions mount as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis strike Saudi energy sites
subheadline: Houthis claim strikes on Saudi refineries at Ras Tanura and Rabigh and Aramco's Abqaiq facility.
author: Reuters, Web Desk
article_text:
UKMTO reports tanker attacks involving projectiles, explosive devices.
Iran claims downed US drone, destroyed sea drone; US denies losses.
Houthis claim strikes on refineries at Ras Tanura, Rabigh, Abqaiq.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.

An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.

Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.

Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.

In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.

It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.

In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.

US-Iran confrontation extends to maritime operations

Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.

Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.

The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.

Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.

At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.

Houthis open another front against Saudi Arabia

The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.

A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.

The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.

The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.

The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.

More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.

The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.

The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.

The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.

Diplomatic efforts struggle to contain escalation

The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.

Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.

Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.

Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.

Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.

The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.

Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.

Oil markets brace for further disruption

The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.

Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.

For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.

The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.

Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.

With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

article_html:
• UKMTO reports tanker attacks involving projectiles, explosive devices.
  • Iran claims downed US drone, destroyed sea drone; US denies losses.
  • Houthis claim strikes on refineries at Ras Tanura, Rabigh, Abqaiq.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.

An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.

Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.

Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.

In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.

It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.

In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.

US-Iran confrontation extends to maritime operations

Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.

Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.

The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.

Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.

At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.

Houthis open another front against Saudi Arabia

The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.

A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.

The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.

The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.

The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.

More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.

The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.

The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.

The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.

Diplomatic efforts struggle to contain escalation

The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.

Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.

Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.

Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.

Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.

The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.

Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.

Oil markets brace for further disruption

The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.

Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.

For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.

The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.

Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.

With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.

The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.

Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.

With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

headline: Crypto faces billion-dollar reckoning as Binance mega-hack exposes security gaps
subheadline: Industry security experts suspect social-engineering attacks, sophisticated money laundering network involved in latest hack
author: Reuters
article_text:
Record hack at Binance shows urgent need to address crypto security.
US moves to integrate crypto with financial system raise stakes in big hacks.
Coinbase adjusts offline crypto-key storage; Kraken reviews security incidents.

A record $6.3 billion hack of Binance has sent alarm bells ringing across the cryptocurrency industry, prompting exchanges to urgently strengthen their defences and call for greater information-sharing to counter growing security threats.

Coinbase said it had adjusted the systems used to store cryptocurrency keys offline, stressing that the move was made "solely out of an abundance of caution". Kraken, meanwhile, said it was monitoring security incidents across the industry to identify lessons that could help shore up its own defences.

The breach has exposed the risks facing an industry increasingly intertwined with mainstream finance, with analysts and executives warning that exchanges must act swiftly to close security gaps.

The urgency is heightened by President Donald Trump's regulators pushing for deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, potentially amplifying the fallout from attacks in a sector already scarred by major hacks.

"For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately," said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton's head of crypto.

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after Thursday's attack — which analysts blamed on North Korea — and said it would use company funds to cover the losses.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the “complex attack” may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals. The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation.

Rival crypto exchanges moved quickly on Friday to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe

“Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day,” a Kraken spokesperson said.

Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% on Thursday while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5%, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Friday.

"Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly," said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according ​to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.

Hack involves social engineering, money laundering

While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said.

Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks.

In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze $800 million. Bitcoin and Ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins.

Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before.

On Friday, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system.

"We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds," said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X.

GSR's Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: "As we're at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it's obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that."

headline: Nelly reveals Taylor Swift flew him to Houston for brief cameo
subheadline: Nelly says Taylor Swift paid him in McDonald’s bag to perform at Houston show
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Nelly has revealed that Taylor Swift once paid him $50,000 in cash, handed over in a McDonald’s bag, for a guest appearance at one of her concerts.

The rapper shared the story on The Breakfast Club podcast.

He said Swift, who was 21 at the time, called him and asked him to perform at two Houston shows on consecutive nights, part of her 2011 Speak Now World Tour.

Read more: Inside how Taylor Swift treats singer who performs at her concert

Swift told him her team had a modest budget, and offered to cover travel and lodging and pay about $50,000.

She wanted him to perform Hot in Herre, as her dancers had already choreographed a routine to it.

“Can you come down to Houston and just perform it?” she asked. Nelly’s reply was to ask whether the money could be delivered in a McDonald’s bag. “Can you put that in a McDonald’s bag?” he said he asked.

Swift agreed.

Her private G5 jet collected Nelly and his family from St. Louis and flew them to Houston.

After the performance, her manager, Robert Allen, handed him a McDonald’s bag containing the $50,000 in cash.

The visit was short.

“We never even saw the room. We went from the show right back to the airport,” Nelly said. He also recalled Swift keeping a close eye on the clock. “We did it, and she was like, ‘Yo, three minutes, three minutes!’”

For Nelly, the cash was never the point. “The money wasn’t really the issue. I would’ve done it for free,” he said.

Nelly has revealed that Taylor Swift once paid him $50,000 in cash, handed over in a McDonald’s bag, for a guest appearance at one of her concerts.

The rapper shared the story on The Breakfast Club podcast.

He said Swift, who was 21 at the time, called him and asked him to perform at two Houston shows on consecutive nights, part of her 2011 Speak Now World Tour.

Read more: Inside how Taylor Swift treats singer who performs at her concert

Swift told him her team had a modest budget, and offered to cover travel and lodging and pay about $50,000.

She wanted him to perform Hot in Herre, as her dancers had already choreographed a routine to it.

“Can you come down to Houston and just perform it?” she asked. Nelly’s reply was to ask whether the money could be delivered in a McDonald’s bag. “Can you put that in a McDonald’s bag?” he said he asked.

Swift agreed.

Her private G5 jet collected Nelly and his family from St. Louis and flew them to Houston.

After the performance, her manager, Robert Allen, handed him a McDonald’s bag containing the $50,000 in cash.

The visit was short.

“We never even saw the room. We went from the show right back to the airport,” Nelly said. He also recalled Swift keeping a close eye on the clock. “We did it, and she was like, ‘Yo, three minutes, three minutes!’”

For Nelly, the cash was never the point. “The money wasn’t really the issue. I would’ve done it for free,” he said.

headline: Martin Scorsese says Seth Rogen 'ruined' Cleopatra film with Angelina Jolie
subheadline: Martin Scorsese blames 'The Interview' and Sony hack for scrapped Angelina Jolie 'Cleopatra' movie
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Martin Scorsese has said a Cleopatra movie he planned to make with Angelina Jolie was ruined by the fallout from Seth Rogen’s film The Interview.

The director spoke in a nearly 40-minute interview with his daughter Francesca, shared by Tribeca on Thursday.

“We were going to do Cleopatra at one point, and then they made fun of Kim Jong [Un],” he said.

Read more: Martin Scorsese daughter Francesca claps back at trolls after landing TV role

Jolie was to play the lead. “Angelina Jolie, we were going. She was Cleopatra VII. It was going to be really wild,” Scorsese said.

The problem, he explained, was North Korea’s response to The Interview, a satire of the country’s government made by Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

The 2014 hack of Sony Pictures, carried out by a North Korean state-sponsored group, leaked confidential emails, messages and data belonging to Sony employees.

Scorsese said Kim Jong Un “got mad and he blew up everybody at Columbia”, which “ruined Cleopatra.”

He joked that Kim did not have a sense of humour, and told Francesca to “tell Seth.”

No other cast members have been reported for Scorsese’s version, and the studio was not named, though the story implies it was Sony.

After the hack, Sony hired David Scarpa to rewrite the script in 2016, and Denis Villeneuve was reportedly in talks to direct in 2017.

More recently, reports said Villeneuve planned to make the film with Zendaya as Cleopatra, but his commitments, including Dune: Part Three and the next James Bond film, make that unlikely.

David Fincher, James Cameron, Paul Greengrass and Ang Lee have all been reported as attached or considered at different points.

headline: Selma Blair apologises after flight incident arrest: 'So sorry'
subheadline: Selma Blair says she never meant to 'hurt or frighten anyone'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Selma Blair has apologised in an emotional Instagram video, saying she never intended to harm anyone after her arrest following an incident on a flight earlier this month.

The actress posted the video on Friday 30 October, her first public comments since the incident on 11 October.

Read more: Selma Blair breaks cover weeks after shocking flight incident

“Not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone a day in my life,” she said. “To the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, that I frightened, alarmed, I am so sorry.”

Blair said she had stayed quiet because her lawyers told her not to discuss specifics while the legal case is ongoing.

She thanked fans, named her son, Arthur Saint Bleick, and her service dog, Scout, and said she is focusing on her health and her son.

Blair was arrested after allegedly punching and biting flight attendants on a Delta flight to New York’s JFK Airport.

She was later accused of kicking a police officer and a nurse while receiving medical attention. She faces two felony counts of second-degree assault, one involving the officer and one involving the nurse, and has pleaded not guilty.

Bail was set at $20,000, and her next court date is 19 January 2027.

Her representative has said Blair experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged behaviour. The flight number and departure city have not been given.

Read more: Selma Blair legal battle puts health in the spotlight

headline: Where have the voters gone?
subheadline: There have been minor reports of protests in KP and arrests, including, of CM and other political figures
author: Bilal I Gilani
article_text:
The recent change of government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa raises a question for anyone interested in Pakistan’s politics and society. Why did the removal of a popular PTI government produce so little visible resistance?

Many analysts expected a strong reaction in the party’s provincial stronghold. PTI-backed candidates had won an overwhelming share of seats in KP, and subsequent Gallup surveys continued to indicate the party’s popularity. Some expected voters to take to the streets. Others anticipated bureaucratic hurdles: resignations, ministers refusing to hand over power, confrontation between provincial police and federal forces and a transition requiring a heavy-handed crackdown.

There have been minor reports of protests in Khyber and arrests, including, worryingly, of the chief minister and other political figures. Yet the larger transition appeared considerably smoother than many had predicted. There was no widespread uprising of the kind that some PTI voices had warned would follow the crossing of a red line.

This article is not an assessment of the legality or morality of the emergency. The question here is analytical: why did the change happen with comparatively little visible resistance, and what does that tell us about politics and public attitudes?

Immediately after the proclamation, Gallup Pakistan conducted a snap poll nationally and in KP. The findings suggested a divided public, with substantial support for and opposition to the emergency and a significant number of respondents unwilling to take a position. On the question of how to respond, around 80% nationally, in KP and within PTI circles favoured a legal route over protest. In other words, data also suggested limited appetite for protest.

I would offer four possible explanations for the gap between the expectation of resistance and what actually happened. First, resentment, disappointment and discontent do not automatically become political action. Individuals can be dissatisfied, neighbourhoods can be dissatisfied, and biradaris can be dissatisfied. To translate that sentiment into collective action capable of producing an outcome, much more is required. This is one reason political parties and other political organisations exist.

Without Imran Khan, the PTI has struggled to act as a cohesive political organisation. Some would argue that, despite its appeal as an iconoclastic force offering a break from dynastic politics and individual whims, the PTI has become even more dependent on one individual than some of the parties it challenged. Much of its vote is identified with Khan personally. Other party leaders, including provincial chief ministers, seem to command little loyalty or political appeal, so the incentive for them to rise is close to non-existent.

That matters for mobilisation. A call to defend Imran Khan himself may carry a very different appeal from a call to defend an individual provincial leader. If the party’s political figures cannot persuade voters that their displacement is equivalent to an attack on Khan, it is much harder to turn his popularity into sustained action on the streets. The event has shown that popularity does not automatically translate into people coming out to protect the government or becoming its defenders unless party mechanics are in place and well oiled.

The second explanation is fragmentation. The PTI leadership has been divided among competing centres of influence: the former and more recently deposed chief ministers and their supporters; figures around Imran Khan’s sisters and his wife; and provincial and national leadership groups. Tensions have also emerged among office holders within the party. The complete silence, even to the extent of press conferences, from the Punjab leg of the PTI is also being questioned. These divisions make collective action harder to coordinate.

Some may see the absence of a stronger party structure as a failure of leadership from Imran Khan. Others may argue that keeping potential successors divided has helped preserve Khan’s central position. The latter is a possible interpretation, not an established account of his motives. Whatever the explanation, the result is that a party with an enormous popular following has struggled to present a unified organisational response.

The 2024 election showed the strength of voters’ commitment, even when the establishment went against the PTI. But an election and a sustained protest make different demands. Voters can make an individual decision in a polling booth; a successful protest movement requires leadership, coordination, resources, and a shared strategy that goes far beyond casting a single vote.

A third possibility concerns the constitution’s place in the public imagination. Even where democratic values are not fully embedded, the idea of constitutional procedure and rule of law may retain legitimacy. The emergency was presented through a formal constitutional process involving presidential proclamation and parliamentary approval. That appearance may have encouraged officials to comply and some citizens to favour legal remedies.

The fourth point is that the PTI’s seat dominance is easily mistaken for unanimous support. The party and its supporters often cite their overwhelming share of seats as evidence that virtually the whole province stands behind them.

Yet, on the estimate cited here, PTI-backed candidates received around 45% of the vote in KP in the 2024 election, while the remainder went to other candidates and parties. The JUI, on the same account, was a distant second at around 18%. These figures require confirmation against the relevant election results and vote denominator.

Voters who chose other parties do not necessarily actively oppose the PTI or support its removal. It does mean that a near-monopoly of assembly seats should not be confused with unanimous public opinion.

All four explanations operate in an environment in which protest can be costly. Arrests, repression and uncertainty about personal safety shape the calculations of voters and political workers. Repression alone, however, may not explain the full absence of political expression. The four reasons shared earlier have played a crucial role.

Nor is the absence of a mass uprising unique to the PTI. The removal of elected governments in Pakistan has often failed to produce a mobilisation proportional to their electoral support. Nawaz Sharif’s removal in the 1999 military coup is one example. Earlier dismissals of elected governments, including those of Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif, also provide grounds to examine the limits of public resistance. The PTI’s claims of exceptional popularity did not necessarily exempt it from the conditions that constrained other parties when they lost power. PTI leadership, including Imran Khan, has perhaps misjudged this limitation.

For the PTI, the experience suggests that confrontation without dialogue — with the establishment and with other political actors — has limited prospects. For the establishment, the orderly transition may show an immediate advantage. It should not be interpreted as a blank cheque or proof that the underlying dispute has disappeared.

In the longer run, the grievances of the people represented by the PTI cannot be resolved simply through administrative control. They require political engagement and reform, including reflection within state institutions.

The writer is executive director of Gallup Pakistan and holds a Masters degree from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), London.
